segments.narration: An empty iron locomotive vanished into a 1912 Belgian tunnel. Seconds later, track bells began ringing miles down the line, alerting stationmasters to a phantom cargo barreling through the dark.

The massive iron engine breached a locked siding switch, defying every safety interlock designed to stop unauthorized movement. No driver sat at the copper throttle, yet the boiler pressure kept climbing into the danger zone.
Railway dispatch logs showed zero telegraph signals sent to the crew. How does a multi-ton machine pilot itself past four active stations without hitting a single red signal?

Investigators eventually discovered the regulator valve had been jammed open by a warped brass lever heated to extreme temperatures. When the crew had abandoned the overheating cab moments earlier, the expanding metal effectively locked the throttle wide open.

The runaway engine was stopped only when it hit a dead-end maintenance spur and derailed in a cloud of white steam. Could a simple piece of warped metal really turn a dead train into a driverless ghost?
